questions.stem: An ecological hazard differs from a natural hazard such as a cyclone because it results mainly from:
options: biological processes, often worsened by people
movements of the Earth's tectonic plates and volcanoes
extreme weather in the atmosphere such as storms
changes in the Earth's orbit around the sun
questions.explanation: Ecological hazards arise from living things, such as invasive species, pathogens and their vectors, and from pollutants affecting the biosphere. Human activity often spreads or worsens them.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an eco-hazard affecting the physical environment, rather than a disease affecting human health?
options: a malaria outbreak in a tropical village
an invasive weed spreading across grazing land
an outbreak of dengue fever in a city
a seasonal influenza epidemic
questions.explanation: Eco-hazards include plant and animal invasions and pollution of land, air, water and living things. Dengue, influenza and malaria are diseases affecting human health.

questions.stem: Cane toads were introduced to Queensland in 1935 to control beetles in sugar cane, then spread across northern Australia. Which process made them an ecological hazard?
options: a natural disaster caused by flooding in the sugar-growing districts
an animal invasion, toxic to native animals, with few predators
a pollutant leaking into groundwater from sugar cane processing mills
a vector-borne disease spread by mosquitoes between cane farms
questions.explanation: With few predators and highly toxic glands, cane toads spread rapidly and killed native predators such as quolls and goannas that ate them. They failed to control the cane beetles they were introduced for.

questions.stem: Prickly pear covered millions of hectares of Queensland and New South Wales by the 1920s. It was largely brought under control by releasing the Cactoblastis moth. This is an example of:
options: biological control of an invasive plant
chemical control using broad-scale spraying
mechanical control by ploughing every paddock
prevention by banning imports of all plants
questions.explanation: Cactoblastis caterpillars feed on prickly pear, and after releases began in 1926 the infestation collapsed. Biological control can work well but carries the risk of the control agent becoming a pest, as cane toads did.

questions.stem: Red imported fire ants were detected in Brisbane in 2001. Why are they considered a serious ecological hazard?
options: they only live in deserts, so they compete with no native species
painful stings and harm to wildlife, farming and infrastructure
they carry malaria and spread it to people in urban areas
they pollute the atmosphere with smoke when nests are disturbed
questions.explanation: Fire ants sting people, pets and livestock, prey on native species and damage crops and electrical equipment. Their spread is a major biosecurity concern for Australia.

questions.stem: When a cargo ship leaked oil off Moreton Island during Cyclone Hamish in 2009, oil washed onto beaches. This is an example of a pollutant affecting the:
options: atmosphere only
cryosphere and atmosphere
hydrosphere and biosphere
lithosphere only
questions.explanation: Oil pollutes water (hydrosphere) and coats birds, marine life and coastal vegetation (biosphere). It also contaminated beach sediments, but the main impacts were on water and living things.

questions.stem: Mercury released by industry enters waterways, is absorbed by small organisms and becomes more concentrated in fish higher up the food chain. This process is called:
options: desertification
soil salinisation
biomagnification
eutrophication
questions.explanation: Biomagnification concentrates persistent pollutants at each trophic level, so top predators and the people who eat them receive the highest doses. Eutrophication is nutrient enrichment of water.

questions.stem: Smoke haze from land clearing fires in Indonesia spreading over neighbouring countries is an example of pollution in which part of the Earth system?
options: the hydrosphere
the cryosphere
the atmosphere
the lithosphere
questions.explanation: Haze is air pollution in the atmosphere that harms human health across borders. Pollutants can then settle onto land and water, affecting other spheres.

questions.stem: A vector-borne disease is one that:
options: is carried between hosts by an organism, such as a mosquito
spreads only through contaminated food that people eat
is passed directly from parents to children at birth
is caused by lack of a vitamin in a person's diet
questions.explanation: Vectors such as mosquitoes and ticks carry pathogens from one host to another. Dengue, malaria and Ross River virus are mosquito-borne diseases.

questions.stem: In Australia, the main vector of dengue is the Aedes aegypti mosquito. Where is it mainly found?
options: only in Antarctic research stations
parts of Queensland, mostly in the north
Tasmania and alpine Victoria
the whole of southern Australia
questions.explanation: Aedes aegypti lives in warm, humid parts of Queensland and breeds in containers around homes. Its range defines where local dengue transmission can occur in Australia.

questions.stem: Australia was declared free of malaria by the World Health Organization in 1981. Why do occasional cases still occur?
options: malaria is spread by cane toads living in northern Queensland
malaria spreads through drinking water in all Australian cities
the malaria parasite lives naturally in Australian soils
travellers return infected from countries with malaria
questions.explanation: Imported cases occur in people infected overseas. Anopheles mosquitoes that can carry malaria still live in northern Australia, so cases are monitored to prevent local spread.

questions.stem: Two towns have Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. One has many rainwater tanks without screens and frequent arrivals of travellers from dengue-affected countries. In hazard terms, this town has higher:
options: magnitude, because each mosquito carries more virus
resilience, because more people live in the town
frequency, because the climate is cooler there
risk, as exposure and vulnerability are both higher
questions.explanation: Unscreened water containers increase mosquito breeding (exposure), and imported cases bring the virus. Risk combines the hazard with exposure and vulnerability.

questions.stem: Which factor most increases a community's vulnerability to a vector-borne disease outbreak?
options: poor access to medical care and poor waste management
a high level of preparedness and fast emergency responses
low population density and well-maintained housing
cool, dry conditions for most of the year
questions.explanation: Lack of health care delays diagnosis and treatment, and uncollected waste holds water where mosquitoes breed. Preparedness, good housing and cooler, drier conditions reduce risk.

questions.stem: Why is the risk from the same ecological hazard often much greater in a less developed country than in Australia?
options: Australia has no climate suitable for any disease vectors
weaker health care, housing and sanitation raise vulnerability
the hazard itself is always biologically different in each country
less developed countries never have any mosquito control programs
questions.explanation: Risk depends on vulnerability as well as the hazard. Access to clinics, piped water, screens and waste collection reduce exposure and harm, and these vary with economic development.

questions.stem: A map shows Queensland shaded where Aedes aegypti has been recorded, with dots for dengue cases. The shaded area is best described as:
options: the ecological hazard zone for local transmission
the area where every resident has been infected with dengue
the zone where cyclones are most likely to make landfall
the area with the highest population density in the state
questions.explanation: The vector's range marks where dengue can spread locally if the virus is introduced. Cases may also be reported elsewhere from travellers, without local spread.

questions.stem: Biosecurity authorities map the area infested by fire ants and set movement controls on soil, hay and mulch inside it. Why does mapping the hazard zone matter?
options: it shows exactly which ant nest will form next in each street
it removes the need for any treatment of known infestations
it proves that fire ants cannot spread outside the mapped area
it targets surveillance and controls where spread is likely
questions.explanation: Mapping lets agencies concentrate treatment and restrict movement of materials that can carry ants, slowing spread. Ants can still spread beyond the zone, so surveillance continues.

questions.stem: A GIS layer of dengue cases is overlaid on a layer of neighbourhoods by income. Cases cluster in areas with older housing and many unscreened water containers. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: dengue cases are randomly spread with no spatial pattern
newer housing areas have no mosquitoes of any kind present
housing and household factors are linked to exposure there
income alone causes dengue, regardless of mosquitoes or the virus
questions.explanation: Spatial overlays reveal associations, here between housing conditions and cases. Correlation needs careful interpretation: the mechanism is more breeding sites, not income itself.

questions.stem: An invasive weed spreads slowly over many years before landholders notice it. In terms of severity factors, this hazard has a:
options: rapid speed of onset and short duration
high frequency and short duration
random sequence and rapid onset
slow speed of onset and long duration
questions.explanation: Many eco-hazards build up gradually and persist for decades, which can delay responses until eradication is impossible. Sudden hazards such as storms are rapid onset.

questions.stem: Dengue outbreaks in North Queensland usually occur in the warmer, wetter months. This is an example of which severity factor?
options: magnitude
speed of onset
duration
seasonality
questions.explanation: Warm, wet conditions increase mosquito breeding and speed virus development, so outbreaks follow a seasonal pattern that helps target control efforts.

questions.stem: An outbreak spreads to many suburbs over several months, infecting hundreds of people. Compared with a few isolated cases, this event has a greater:
options: speed of onset only
regularity only
random sequencing only
magnitude and duration
questions.explanation: Magnitude refers to the size of the event, such as the number of cases or area affected, and duration to how long it lasts. Both increase the severity of impacts.

questions.stem: Why might climate change increase the risk of dengue in Queensland?
options: lower humidity would make the virus survive longer in water
climate change would remove all water containers from homes
warming could extend the vector's range and season
cooler temperatures would make mosquitoes breed much faster
questions.explanation: Warming can expand areas suitable for Aedes aegypti, lengthen the breeding season and shorten the time the virus takes to develop in the mosquito, raising transmission risk.

questions.stem: How can climate change affect the severity of invasive species as an eco-hazard?
options: by making all invasive species extinct within a few years
by preventing any species from moving to new places
by reducing disturbances that let weeds establish
by letting some species spread into newly suitable areas
questions.explanation: Shifts in temperature and rainfall can open new areas to invasive species, and extreme events such as floods and fires disturb habitats, giving invaders space to establish.

questions.stem: Dengue fever is caused by a virus with four types, or serotypes. Why does this matter for public health?
options: only one type can infect people; the others infect cattle
the four types are spread by four different animals
infection with a second type can cause severe illness
infection with one type gives immunity to all four types
questions.explanation: Infection gives lasting immunity only to that serotype, and a later infection with a different one carries a higher risk of severe dengue. This complicates vaccines and outbreaks.

questions.stem: Most dengue cases recorded in Queensland are acquired overseas. Local outbreaks begin when:
options: infected cane toads move into suburbs during the wet season
the virus is carried south by winds from Papua New Guinea
a local Aedes aegypti bites an infected traveller, then others
the virus spreads through the town water supply after heavy rain
questions.explanation: A local Aedes aegypti mosquito that bites an infected traveller can pass the virus to other people, starting local transmission. This is why travellers with fever are asked to avoid mosquito bites.

questions.stem: Wolbachia is a bacterium that, when established in Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, reduces their ability to transmit dengue. How has the World Mosquito Program used it in North Queensland?
options: by releasing fish that eat Wolbachia-infected mosquito larvae
by releasing Wolbachia mosquitoes to breed with local ones
by spraying Wolbachia over towns to kill all adult mosquitoes
by vaccinating residents with Wolbachia to prevent infection
questions.explanation: Released Wolbachia mosquitoes mate with wild ones, and the bacterium spreads through the population over generations. Once established, it persists without further releases.

questions.stem: After Wolbachia mosquitoes were established across Townsville from 2014, local dengue transmission virtually stopped in the treated areas. Which feature makes this strategy especially sustainable?
options: it sustains itself once established, without insecticides
it must be repeated every week, providing permanent local employment
it eliminates every mosquito species from the environment for ever
it works only in cold climates where mosquitoes are naturally rare
questions.explanation: Because Wolbachia passes from mother to offspring, it maintains itself in the mosquito population, with low long-term cost and no chemical spraying. It does not wipe out mosquitoes.

questions.stem: A large trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, found dengue cases were about 77% lower in areas with Wolbachia mosquitoes. Why is this result important for evaluating the North Queensland strategy?
options: it suggests the method increases dengue in tropical cities
it shows the method works in a large, high-dengue city
it proves that Wolbachia only works outside Australia
it shows that dengue has been eradicated worldwide
questions.explanation: The randomised trial gave strong evidence in a setting with far more dengue than Queensland, supporting the method's wider use. Evidence from different places strengthens an evaluation.

questions.stem: Which household action reduces the risk of dengue in North Queensland?
options: leaving rainwater tanks open so the water stays fresh
emptying or covering water containers around the yard
planting more pot plants with saucers full of water
storing old tyres outdoors where rain can collect
questions.explanation: Aedes aegypti breeds in small containers of standing water near homes. Removing or covering them, and screening tanks, cuts breeding sites.

questions.stem: Queensland Health responds to a local dengue case by spraying inside nearby homes and treating breeding sites. In hazard management terms, this is mainly a:
options: mitigation of climate change
response to contain an outbreak
long-term prevention measure
recovery measure after an outbreak
questions.explanation: Targeted spraying around cases is an emergency response that stops infected mosquitoes passing the virus on. Wolbachia and container removal are longer-term prevention.

questions.stem: Which is a secondary impact of a dengue outbreak in a tourist town?
options: fever and joint pain in infected people
mosquitoes biting residents in their yards
the virus multiplying in a person's blood
lost tourism income as visitors stay away
questions.explanation: Primary impacts are the direct effects of infection on people. Secondary impacts follow from them, such as lost income, health care costs and reduced tourism.

questions.stem: A student proposes action to reduce dengue risk in a North Queensland town. Which proposal is best supported by evidence and most likely to be sustainable?
options: drain every wetland in the region to remove all mosquito habitat
maintain and monitor Wolbachia, plus container clean-ups
spray insecticide over the whole town every day, all year round
ban all travellers from entering Queensland during the wet season
questions.explanation: Combining an established biological control with community action and surveillance is effective and low impact. Blanket spraying harms other species and builds resistance, and travel bans are impractical.

questions.stem: Why is early detection so important in managing an invasive species?
options: eradication is only feasible while infestations are small
invasive species become harmless once they spread widely
late detection always makes eradication cheaper and easier
early detection is only useful for diseases, not species
questions.explanation: Small, localised infestations can sometimes be eradicated; once a species spreads widely, management usually shifts to costly long-term containment.

questions.stem: Australia inspects incoming cargo, mail and passengers' luggage for pests and diseases. This biosecurity approach is best described as:
options: recovery after an outbreak
response during an outbreak
adaptation to climate change
prevention at the border
questions.explanation: Border biosecurity aims to stop pests and diseases arriving, the cheapest and most effective form of management. Once established, they are far harder to control.

questions.stem: Which data would best show the effectiveness of a program to control fire ants in South East Queensland?
options: rainfall totals at Brisbane Airport during the program
the population of Brisbane recorded at the latest census
change in infested area and new detections over years
the number of brochures about fire ants printed in a single year
questions.explanation: Effectiveness is measured by outcomes such as whether the infested area is shrinking or spreading, tracked over time with mapping and surveillance data.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of an agency at the individual or community scale helping to manage an ecological hazard?
options: residents reporting suspected fire ant nests
a United Nations agency coordinating global disease data
the national government funding border biosecurity
a state government passing new biosecurity laws
questions.explanation: Community reporting greatly increases surveillance, helping detect new outbreaks early. The other actions are by international, national or state agencies.
